text: Lesson eighty-six, Running Totals and Moving Averages. Chapter ten, Window and Ranking Functions.

Everything in this chapter has been building toward this. Sum of total due, over order by order date, rows between unbounded preceding and current row, as running total due. That frame means every row from the start of the result set up to and including the current row. So for each order, this adds up every total due value so far — a running total, one query, no loop, no self-join.

A moving average is a running total's sliding cousin. Average of total due, over order by order date, rows between 6 preceding and current row, as seven row moving average. Instead of growing to include every row from the start, this frame slides along with the current row, always covering a fixed number of rows — the current one plus the six before it, seven rows total.

And exactly like every other window function in this chapter, adding partition by sales person I.D. restarts the running total at zero for each salesperson, instead of accumulating across the whole table. Why rows, and not range? Both of these need a frame measured in physical rows — the last seven rows, not every row sharing the same value. Range would behave unpredictably the moment two rows tied on the order-by column.

Chapter ten built a complete toolkit. OVER and PARTITION BY as the foundation. Row number, rank, dense rank, and NTILE for ranking and bucketing. LAG and LEAD for comparing neighboring rows. FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE for the edges of a window. ROWS versus RANGE for controlling the frame. And now running totals and moving averages, tying it all together.

Chapter eleven moves into Performance Tuning — execution plans, indexes, and the comparative topics, like joins versus subqueries, that look at everything you've learned so far from a speed perspective. See you there.
